title: Narada fetches water
hook: the sage Narada asks to see maya, and Vishnu sends him for a cup of water
carry: maya: real while it lasts, not on its own

segments.voice: Yesterday: Advaita's rope and snake. A lamp, not a stick: knowing sets you free. Today, a story about the dark itself, and the Hindu word for it.

The sage Narada, who wanders the worlds singing God's names, once asked Vishnu a favor. Show me your maya, he said: the power that makes the world seem what it seems. Vishnu smiled and said, later. First, bring me some water from that village. So Narada walks down to the village and knocks on a door. A young woman opens it. And Narada forgets all about the water.
screen: `SHOW ME YOUR MAYA.` → `FIRST, BRING ME WATER.` → `A DOOR OPENS.`

segments.voice: He stays. He marries her. Years pass: children, a farm, a home. Then the rains won't stop, the river rises, and a flood sweeps everything away. Narada is on the bank, alone and weeping, when a voice behind him says: Narada, where's my water? I've been waiting. It's Vishnu, and almost no time has passed. That, the story says, is maya. Not that Narada's years were nothing. He loved, he worked, he grieved, and all of it was real while he was in it. But it wasn't the last word, and it wasn't real on its own. People hear maya and think Hindus believe the world is fake, so nothing matters. That's not what Shankara's school says. Later Advaita teachers, building on him, sort it into levels. The snake on the rope, or a dream: real only while you're mistaken. The everyday world: rent, school, your grandmother's birthday, fully real for every practical purpose. Here promises matter, cruelty hurts, and duty is duty. And Brahman alone, not two. Their careful word for the world is mithya: not unreal like a square circle, not real on its own like Brahman. Real to live in, and resting on something deeper. So the teaching excuses you from nothing. Tradition remembers Shankara himself walking India, teaching, and coming home to his mother when she was dying. What changes is the grip. And today? When a school year, a fight or a long scroll swallows you whole, Hindus have a word for that pull. You still show up for all of it. You just remember who sent you for water.
screen: `A LIFE, THEN: WHERE'S MY WATER?` · `MAYA: REAL WHILE IT LASTS.` · `DREAM, DAILY LIFE, BRAHMAN.` · `MITHYA: REAL, BUT NOT ON ITS OWN.` · then, large: `REAL WHILE IT LASTS.`

segments.voice: Find something you've owned for years: a mug, a book, a bracelet. Hold it. Remember when it was new to you, and let the years since pass through your mind, the people, the places, the worries that felt huge. Then come back to right now, to the hands holding it. All of that happened, and here you still are, the one holding it. Rest there for a few breaths.
Advaita and maya: the world is real while it lasts, like Narada's years in the village. Its careful word is mithya: fully real to live in, not real on its own.
Keep this one: maya, real while it lasts, not on its own. That's day two eighty-three.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers tell stories like Narada's to explain maya, and Advaita teachers explain the world as mithya, dependent reality, with levels of reality (the apparent, the practical and the absolute) so that ethics and duty stay fully in place while students contemplate non-duality.

original.note: Sanskrit: maya, often translated 'illusion'; the power by which the one appears as the many.

trapdoor: what you thought: maya means Hindus believe the world is fake.
what it means: the world is real to live in but not real on its own, like Narada's years in the village; in Advaita it's mithya.

what a scholar hears: Narada's lesson in maya has Puranic versions (in the Devi Bhagavata, Narada becomes a woman and lives a whole life) and Ramakrishna's telling with the water; the three levels (pāramārthika, vyāvahārika, prātibhāsika) are systematized by post-Shankara Advaitins; mithya is 'other than real and unreal' (sad-asad-vilakṣaṇa).

sources.ref: Narada's lesson in maya: a traditional story told in many versions, with a Puranic version (Devi Bhagavata Purana, where Narada becomes a woman) and popular tellings with the errand for water, among them Ramakrishna's (the god is Vishnu or Rama, depending on the telling)
Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya (the everyday and the ultimate standpoints)
traditional lives of Shankara (Shankara-digvijaya): his return to his dying mother
later Advaita works on the three levels of reality and mithya (e.g. Vedanta Paribhasha, Panchadashi)
